documents.title: DD15 Won't Start Troubleshooting
documents.summary: TruckFixHub DD15 evidence: Separate no-crank from crank-no-start before replacing parts. If the engine cranks but will not start, verify adequate cranking speed and battery voltage; check fuel supply and investigate loss of prime, restriction, air intrusion or recent fuel-system work; use diagnostic data to verify the engine controller is seeing information required for starting; inspect accessible engine-harness connectors and wiring for damage, corrosion, loose terminals or recent disturbance; record SPN/FMI codes and determine which are active, and do not assume a component named by a code is automatically defective. If the no-start began after batteries, fuel filters, wiring, CPC/ECM work or another repair, begin by checking what changed. Missing module data, unusual dash behavior or multiple communication faults deserve electrical/network diagnosis before expensive engine parts are replaced. Do not bypass safety systems or loosen high-pressure fuel components to check for fuel.

documents.title: Cummins X15 Won't Start Troubleshooting
documents.summary: TruckFixHub X15 evidence: Separate no-crank from crank-no-start before chasing fuel or sensors. If the X15 cranks but will not start, verify cranking speed and battery voltage are adequate; check fuel supply, filters and recent fuel-system service and investigate restriction, air intrusion or loss of prime rather than guessing at expensive components; use diagnostic software/data to confirm the ECM is receiving the engine information needed during cranking; inspect accessible harnesses, connectors, power and grounds for damage, corrosion, looseness or recent disturbance; record all active Cummins fault information before clearing codes. If the problem began after a fuel-filter change, battery replacement, wiring repair or engine work, inspect what was just touched. Fuel-pressure and fuel-delivery complaints should be verified using applicable Cummins procedures and service information rather than treated as automatic component replacements. Do not bypass safety systems or loosen high-pressure fuel components to check for fuel.

documents.title: Semi-Truck Engine Cranks But Won't Start
documents.summary: TruckFixHub general crank-no-start evidence: A true crank-no-start means the engine is rotating at a reasonable cranking speed; slow or labored cranking points back toward batteries, cables, connections, starter load or mechanical resistance. Useful observations include whether it quit while driving or failed after shutdown, whether it attempts to fire, cranking speed consistency, warning/security messages, engine-controller communication, active SPN/FMI or manufacturer faults, plausible ECM engine speed while cranking, recent service, and known fuel level/condition. Diagnostic path: verify adequate battery voltage, cable integrity and cranking speed under load; verify engine-controller power and communication; evaluate engine-speed information using the exact engine OEM procedure; evaluate fuel supply restriction, air intrusion, priming, supply-pump operation, filters, commanded versus actual rail pressure and injector/control conditions as applicable to that engine; if electronic and fuel requirements are met, approved procedures may be needed for intake restriction, valve timing, compression or other mechanical causes. Required pressures and tests vary by engine family. Do not replace a crank sensor, fuel pump, injectors or ECM merely because those parts can cause a no-start; confirm the failed condition first. Follow OEM fuel-system safety procedures and do not use starting fluid unless specifically permitted by the manufacturer and approved procedure.

documents.title: DEF, SCR & NOx Sensor Troubleshooting
documents.summary: TruckFixHub verified DEF/SCR/NOx evidence: Treat DEF level warnings, DEF quality warnings, SCR performance faults, NOx-sensor faults and derate/inducement as related aftertreatment symptoms that still require separate diagnosis. Capture the complete active and inactive fault set, exact dash warning, operating conditions, recent repairs, DEF refill history and which sensor/location the manufacturer diagnostic information identifies. A full DEF tank does not prove the system is healthy, and a warning after a refill is evidence rather than proof that the fluid caused the fault. A NOx-related code does not automatically prove the NOx sensor is defective; manufacturer diagnostics may require checking electrical supply, grounds, wiring/connectors, sensor plausibility, exhaust conditions and related aftertreatment faults. An SCR fault does not automatically mean the SCR catalyst needs replacement. Derate is an outcome rather than a diagnosis; record the earliest warning because it can be more useful than the final derate message. Do not clear codes before recording them. Depending on the fault, qualified diagnosis may include operating data and code history, DEF-system information, sensor plausibility, electrical power/grounds, wiring/connectors, dosing operation, exhaust-system conditions and manufacturer-specific SCR tests. Follow current OEM procedures and never defeat emissions or engine-protection logic.

documents.title: Truck Won't Regen / Parked Regen Troubleshooting
documents.summary: TruckFixHub verified regen evidence: A parked regeneration that will not start or complete does not automatically mean the DPF needs replacement. Before clearing anything, record every active SPN/FMI. Verify the engine is at the required operating temperature, check fuel level and OEM-specific parked-regen enable conditions, confirm parking-brake, transmission/neutral and other safety interlocks are satisfied, and look for active engine or aftertreatment faults that can inhibit regeneration. Where appropriate inspect DPF differential-pressure sensing tubes and wiring, and review soot load and regeneration history with compatible diagnostic software. If the truck repeatedly requests regeneration, diagnose why soot is accumulating or regeneration is ineffective; investigation can include engine-out soot production, exhaust temperature, pressure sensing, dosing, aftertreatment condition and duty cycle. Do not force a regen blindly: high soot load, active faults or damaged aftertreatment components can require OEM-directed testing or service before regeneration is appropriate. Follow the engine manufacturer's procedure.

documents.title: Semi Truck Won't Build Air Pressure
documents.summary: TruckFixHub verified air-system evidence: First distinguish no pressure increase, slow build, pressure that builds then falls, pressure that stops at a certain point, and different behavior between primary and secondary gauges. Common investigation areas include large or continuous leaks in lines, fittings, valves, chambers or connected systems; air-compressor output and drive concerns; governor and compressor-control operation; air dryer, purge valve and associated plumbing; restricted or leaking lines; reservoir plumbing; and brake-system valves or other air-operated accessories. Repeated dryer purging or leakage is useful evidence but does not by itself prove the dryer failed because leakage elsewhere can cause frequent compressor cycling. Record both gauge readings, response to engine RPM, obvious leakage, dryer behavior, spring-brake release, recent air-system work and whether pressure is lost while parked. If pressure builds normally and then drops, diagnose air loss/leak behavior rather than assuming the compressor cannot produce air. Do not drive a truck that cannot maintain safe air pressure, and never bypass low-air warnings or spring brakes.

documents.title: Semi Truck Losing Air Pressure / Air Leak Troubleshooting
documents.summary: TruckFixHub verified air-loss evidence: Determine when pressure drops: engine off with brakes released, during service-brake application, with parking brakes released, while the engine is running, or after shutdown. Watch both primary and secondary gauges because one circuit dropping while the other stays relatively stable is important diagnostic information. Common inspection areas include air lines, hoses, fittings and connections; brake chambers and plumbing; relay, protection and control valves; air dryer and purge-valve area; reservoirs, drains and tank connections; cab, suspension and other air-operated accessories; and trailer supply/connections when attached. If the leak appears only with brake application, record whether it occurs with light or full application and whether it is loudest at a wheel position. Repeated dryer purging does not automatically prove the dryer failed because another leak can cause frequent compressor cycling. For overnight loss, record starting pressure, ending pressure, elapsed time and whether a trailer was connected. Do not operate a truck that cannot maintain safe air pressure, do not crawl under an unsecured vehicle, and never bypass low-air warnings or spring brakes.

documents.title: Semi Truck Charging & Battery Problems
documents.summary: TruckFixHub verified charging-system evidence: Separate battery condition and state of charge, charging-system performance, excessive resistance in cables/grounds/connections, and an electrical load that remains after shutdown before replacing parts. Record whether the truck becomes dead after sitting, while driving or shortly after shutdown; whether cranking is slow, clicking or completely dead; charging/battery warnings; recent battery, alternator, starter, cable, ground or accessory work; and whether the problem is intermittent. Inspect the battery bank, terminals, interconnects, cables and grounds for looseness, damage or corrosion. Evaluate battery condition using the applicable battery or vehicle procedure. Verify charging-system operation under the conditions where the complaint occurs; low batteries alone do not prove the alternator failed because wiring, grounds, drive concerns, control strategy and electrical load can affect charging. Check the complete high-current path and use the applicable procedure for voltage-drop testing. If batteries discharge while parked, investigate key-off draw after allowing vehicle modules to enter their normal sleep state. Exact voltage, load-test and allowable-draw specifications vary by vehicle and components, so use correct service information rather than universal numbers. Heavy-duty battery systems can deliver very high current; follow OEM/component safety procedures and do not disconnect or bypass charging components as an improvised test.
